planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil, allowing wide clearance since the arching branches will eventually sweep the ground on all sides.

directions: This cascading sport of the species forms long, pendulous branches that drape downward from a central leader, eventually creating a tent-like mass of foliage wide enough to walk beneath on mature specimens. Stake the leading shoot when young to establish height before the weeping habit takes over, and site it where its eventual spread will not crowd structures or paths. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, since dense shade beneath the canopy will prevent grass or groundcovers from persisting underneath. It is slow-growing but extremely long-lived, often becoming a dramatic specimen centerpiece over many decades.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil, choosing a permanent site since beech resents transplanting once established.

directions: One of the oldest and most intensely colored of the purple-leaved beech selections, this nineteenth-century English introduction holds near-black purple foliage through summer better than many newer purple cultivars, which often fade toward bronze-green by midsummer heat. It forms a dense, broadly pyramidal to oval canopy and casts heavy shade, so underplanting beneath a mature tree is rarely successful. Grow it in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the darkest leaf color, since shaded plants trend greener. Give it generous room from its first planting, as it dislikes root disturbance and resents being moved later in life.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil; established plants tolerate dry, rocky sites poorly suited to most other flowering shrubs.

directions: Native to the limestone coasts of South Australia, this low, spreading shrub carries small, leathery leaves and an abundance of dangling, narrow tubular flowers in salmon-pink, coral, or occasionally white from autumn through spring. It is one of the parent species behind many popular Correa garden hybrids, but the wild species itself makes a tougher, more compact groundcover or low border plant where space is tight. Grow it in sharply-drained, low-fertility soil, since rich garden soil and high-phosphorus fertilizer both tend to shorten its life. It handles coastal exposure, salt spray, and extended dry spells with ease once its roots are established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with some shelter from strong wind and afternoon sun.

directions: Selected from seedlings grown by a northern California nursery, this cultivar was chosen because it begins flowering within a couple of years of propagation rather than the decade or more typical of seedling dove trees, so gardeners see its large white bracts, which hang beneath the branches like handkerchiefs or resting doves, far sooner. It forms a pyramidal small tree with cinnamon-toned bark and yellow-to-red fall color. Plant in part shade in hot summer climates and full sun where summers are mild, keeping roots consistently moist but never waterlogged. Shelter from strong wind helps protect the papery bracts during the late-spring bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors after nicking the hard seed coat and soaking overnight; transplant out after frost once soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems.

directions: This fully double-flowered selection of the Southeast Asian butterfly pea packs extra layers of deep indigo-blue petals into each bloom, giving a fuller, rose-like flower compared to the five-petaled single form, though it lacks the fertile pods that make the single type popular as a food-dye source. Grow it as a twining vine on a trellis, arbor, or fence in full sun with consistently moist, well-drained soil. In frost-free climates it persists as a woody-based perennial; elsewhere, grow it as a fast warm-season annual vine, since it flowers prolifically from summer through first frost. Pinching young vines encourages bushier growth and more flowering side-shoots.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into moist, humus-rich soil; it tolerates light frost once established but prefers a sheltered, part-shaded site while young.

directions: Also sold as carrol or neverbreak, this rainforest tree from the subtropical gullies of eastern Australia bears small, glossy, leathery leaves that release a sweet, cinnamon-like fragrance when crushed, and masses of fluffy cream flowers that blanket the canopy in midsummer. It tolerates clipping well and is frequently grown as a dense screening hedge or espalier as an alternative to lemon myrtle where a milder, spicier scent is preferred. Plant in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in part shade when young, moving to more sun as the tree matures and its bark develops an attractive mottled grey patina. Leaves can be dried for a cinnamon-scented tea, though the tree is grown primarily as a hedge or specimen plant.

planting.note: Plant grafted or cutting-grown stock in spring into lean, fast-draining, rocky or sandy soil on a slope if possible; avoid summer irrigation once established, since wet roots in warm soil are usually fatal.

directions: A hybrid selection between the two California flannel bush species, this cultivar produces an especially heavy spring flush of large, fuzzy, orange-blushed yellow flowers that often continues sporadically into summer. Like other flannelbushes, its leaves, stems, and seed capsules are covered in fine hairs that can irritate skin and eyes, so gloves and eye protection are worth using when pruning. Plant it on a slope or raised, gritty site where water drains away quickly, since it is notoriously intolerant of any summer moisture around its roots once established in the garden. Prune only lightly and right after flowering, as it blooms on the previous year's wood and resents hard cutting back.
